Use mapped_column(ForeignKey("customers.id")) for customer_id and relationship() for related objects or collections. Customer.orders navigates to orders; Order.customer navigates to the customer. blocks.title: Stored reference versus Python navigation
blocks.alt_text: The stored orders.customer_id reference points to customers.id. Separate Customer.orders and Order.customer navigation arrows name each other through back_populates.

blocks.text: Order.customer_id represents the stored reference to customers.id. Order.customer represents navigation to a Customer object, while Customer.orders is the counterpart collection. On Customer.orders, back_populates="customer" names Order.customer; on Order.customer, back_populates="orders" names Customer.orders. These names identify counterpart attributes, not merely tables. The paired relationships establish bidirectional in-Python association behavior; they do not determine every later loading or query behavior.

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship
from base import Base

class Customer(Base):
    __tablename__ = "customers"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    orders: Mapped[list["Order"]] = relationship(back_populates="customer")

class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    customer_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("customers.id"))
    customer: Mapped["Customer"] = relationship(back_populates="orders")

blocks.text: Mapped[list["Order"]] declares collection navigation to Order objects; Mapped["Customer"] declares navigation to one Customer object. These annotations supply the related class to relationship(). Quoting the class name lets Customer refer to Order before Order is declared. The customer_id column separately stores the foreign-key reference. Each back_populates value names the relationship attribute on the opposite class.
A relationship attribute does not replace a database foreign-key column. Stored association and object navigation are declared alongside one another.

segments.label: Pair relationship attributes with back_populates
segments.summary: The User/UserAuth example uses single-object navigation, while User/posts connects a user with a collection of posts. Both examples pair relationship attributes through back_populates, with each side naming its counterpart. This establishes bidirectional association behavior between Python objects; it does not mean that database tables immediately synchronize. UserPost.userID separately represents the stored association: its foreign key refers to the identifier of a User row. The example also requires userID to have a value. Single-object navigation alone does not establish database uniqueness.
